narrative.text: The lights in the broadcast hall run hot. You are forty minutes into the press conference when the nerve damage flares — not a warning, just the thing itself. Your hand spasms. The water glass goes off the podium with a crack that fills the room. Six hundred people go silent simultaneously.
Chancellor. Are you unwell? The nation is watching.

She said it quietly but the microphone caught it. My hand is still shaking. The ringing in my left ear is doing what it always does — turning the room into something underwater. The cameras are zoomed in on my face. Whatever I say next is the story.

choices.text: Admit it. 'The attempt on my life left scars. I govern with them.'
Attack. 'How dare you question my health while Veltrians are suffering.'

narrative.text: The room stays quiet for a moment after I say it. Then someone starts to applaud — one person, then a section, then most of the hall. Nadia writes something on her notepad. The evening broadcast leads with it. Not as a scandal. As a statement. My press secretary calls it the best thirty seconds of the term. I don't argue. My hand is still shaking.

Nadia writes it down. Fatigue. She will not print fatigue — she will print what the cameras caught and let the readers decide what fatigue looks like. The glass is still on the floor when I leave. Someone photographed it. By morning the image is everywhere: the podium, the wet floor, the empty space where my composure was.

The room flinches. Nadia does not. She writes it down without expression — the mark of a journalist who expected it. The Iron Covenant will call it strength. The reformists will call it deflection. Both are correct. I walked out of the hall on my own legs, my hand in my pocket, and gave no further comment. The glass stayed on the floor.
